title: [Full Workshop from Microsoft] Github Copilot - The World's Most Widely Adopted AI Developer Tool
talk_summary: A GitHub Copilot hands-on workshop covering IDE completions, inline chat, chat panel, slash commands, and Copilot Workspace, with an impromptu Q&A from a VS Code team member. The most transferable content is the multi-model routing rationale (latency vs quality per surface), the offline eval approach for slash commands, and context-selection mechanics.

takeaways.technique: Per-surface model tiering by latency budget
takeaways.what_they_do: They route different product surfaces to different models based on latency tolerance: fast small model for ghost-text completions, mid model for inline chat, strongest model only for the chat panel where users tolerate waiting.
takeaways.evidence_quote: for completions we're using 3.5 very SM very small context window to say under these 250 milliseconds instant ghost text
takeaways.numbers: ~250ms target for completions; GPT-4 gave 'only a slight lift in quality and only in some languages' for inline chat but users churned on time-to-first-token

takeaways.technique: Small regression eval set per command, run on every change
takeaways.what_they_do: They maintain code-based offline evals for each slash command (fix, docs), with a small test set run on every code change to catch regressions, plus larger cross-repo evals; they note model upgrades often require prompt changes and can regress some languages.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we have a smaller test set that runs generally on each change code change where we test specific patterns if they improve or uh regress

takeaways.technique: Explicit context attachment over implicit inference
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than relying on the model to find relevant code, they expose explicit attach controls (files, symbols) and tell users to select code or attach references; they also surface which references were used so users can verify grounding.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the more explicit if you know what you're talking about just show it to co-pilot just like you would do with anybody else

takeaways.what_they_do: They package frequent prompt patterns (explain, fix, test, doc) as reusable slash commands so users don't re-describe the same task each time, and commands auto-detect framework/folder conventions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: these shortcuts allow you to not be overly prescriptive for very common tasks like fixing books and explaining code

takeaways.technique: Plan-then-edit workspace flow with human-in-loop checkpoints
takeaways.what_they_do: Copilot Workspace starts from a task, breaks it into a plan, lets the user correct plan items before cross-file edits, then produces a diff and can run build steps in a terminal.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it breaks it down into a plan and it allows you to make cross repo uh cross file edits ... keeps the developer in control at every step

takeaways.technique: Fresh conversation per task to avoid context drift
takeaways.what_they_do: They advise starting a new chat for each new task because long histories cause the model to get stuck on earlier concepts.
